items.headline: U.S. Department of Justice Files Legal Brief Urging Court to Find AI Training to Be Fair Use
items.excerpt: In a 20-page 'Statement of Interest,' lawyers for the U.S. Department of Justice told the judge presiding over a closely watched lawsuit that requiring “paid licensing” would “put U.S. AI companies at a competitive disadvantage.” A direct hit on how authors and publishers can price their work as training data.

items.headline: Microsoft says virtually nobody was grabbing NYT articles through its chatbot
items.excerpt: Microsoft's new filing in the New York Times and authors' copyright suit argues that regurgitation of copyrighted text by Copilot was vanishingly rare, a claim that shapes how writers can prove harm from AI training.

items.headline: Anthropic Copyright Settlement: Publishers Are Making Incorrect Claims on Authors’ Payouts
items.excerpt: Authors in the Anthropic class action began receiving settlement notices this week — and some publishers are telling their authors they are entitled to a share when the settlement terms say otherwise. A practical guide to who actually owns the AI-training payout.

items.headline: Widespread Problems as Authors Receive Anthropic Settlement Notices
items.excerpt: Authors and publishers who filed claims in the Anthropic lawsuit should receive a first payment between November 1 and 15, according to a status report filed by class counsel — but the notice rollout is riddled with errors.

items.headline: Trump Administration Files Statement in Support of OpenAI in Copyright Suits
items.excerpt: The Department of Justice took the highly unusual step of filing a “statement of interest” backing OpenAI and Microsoft in the copyright infringement lawsuit brought by the New York Times and author plaintiffs.

items.headline: When Your AI Knows You Too Well: Personalization, Sycophancy, and the Risk of an Intellectual Echo Chamber
items.excerpt: As AI research and writing assistants learn our preferences, they also get better at mirroring our assumptions. Avoiding that outcome, the piece argues, will require more than a better prompt.

items.headline: How Good Are AI Custom-Written Novels?
items.excerpt: Ember Novels shows that AI is increasingly able to develop and carry plot across 300 pages with fewer continuity errors than many AI-generated or AI-assisted books currently on the market.

items.headline: Google rolls out AI chatbots for books, with permission from publishers and authors
items.excerpt: Readers of participating Google Play Books titles can now query the text and generate infographics, audio overviews, quizzes and other interactive features — with publisher and author opt-in.

items.headline: Podcast: We Spoke to an Amazon Worker Destroying Books for AI
items.excerpt: A follow-up to the Amazon-destroying-books-for-AI story, told by a worker inside the scanning operation — plus why a handful of fake names keep appearing across AI-generated papers.

items.headline: We Can Now Track AI-generated Content. It Doesn’t Solve the Real Problem.
items.excerpt: Identifying AI content is now embedded in Claude models. It doesn't solve the problem publishers actually have — and it creates new ones for editors and authors.

items.headline: MIT Warns That AI Can Now Credibly Complete Pretty Much Any Undergrad Assignment
items.excerpt: A new report from MIT's ad hoc AI committee warns that written coursework and textbook-based assessment no longer separate student work from model output, and considers overhauling the educational model.

items.headline: Google Launches AI Tool to Add Interactivity to E-books
items.excerpt: Expert Intelligence lets readers query e-books bought from the Google Play store, and covers more than 100,000 titles — mostly trade nonfiction — from publishers including Penguin Random House, Macmillan and Bloomsbury.

items.headline: AI Use in The Scholarly Kitchen
items.excerpt: An editorial team explains its own disclosure rules after reader pushback on AI use by authors, weighing a Nature piece on the efficacy of AI detection tools against the need to keep experimenting.

items.headline: The AI ‘Ghosts’ Contaminating Academic Publishing
items.excerpt: “The academic record is being quietly haunted” by nonexistent researchers with names like Elena Vasquez and Marcus Chen — hallucinated co-authors now propagating through published papers and citations.

items.headline: Top WSJ Editor Approves AI-Assisted Writing, Says AI Is a “Fact of Modern Life”
items.excerpt: The Wall Street Journal is giving opinion authors the go-ahead to use AI in the writing process without requiring AI disclosures — a marker for how writing craft norms are shifting.

items.headline: Opinion: You Have More Agency Than You Think — Creative Writing and Publishing in the Age of AI
items.excerpt: Indie author Nigel George argues that writers still control the terms on which they use — or refuse — AI tools, and lays out how to build a personal working policy instead of drifting with the hype.

items.headline: Can AI Replace Your Editor? Member Q&A with Michael La Ronn and Sacha Black
items.excerpt: Michael La Ronn and Sacha Black answer member questions on where AI editing actually holds up in a manuscript workflow, plus IngramSpark returns and series cover consistency.
